name: simdjson-oxcaml (simdjson-ox)
workload: Geometric-mean parse throughput (MB/s) across 7 standard JSON corpus fixtures (apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, gsoc-2018, marine_ik, numbers, twitter.json), single P-core pinned, Bechamel/Google Benchmark harness
claimed_speedup: simdjson-ox-tape-reusable geomean 1247.7 MB/s vs rapidjson-dom 1059.7 MB/s (~1.18x faster, derived from page data) and vs nlohmann-json-dom 132.2 MB/s (~9.4x faster, derived from page data); still behind C++ simdjson-dom (3344.5 MB/s) and sajson-dom (1650.9 MB/s)
compiler_and_flags: OCaml 'perf' dune profile (native flags -g, -gno-upstream-dwarf, -gdwarf-inlined-frames, -gdwarf-fidelity high) on OxCaml 5.2.0+ox / Dune 3.22.2; C++ comparators (RapidJSON, nlohmann, sajson, simdjson) built with GCC 15.2.1, CMake Release config
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700K (8 P-core + 4 E-core, 20 logical CPUs), pinned to logical CPU 0 (P-core) via taskset, performance governor, ASLR disabled, Fedora Linux 43, kernel 6.19.14-200.fc43.x86_64
tradeoffs: Still ~2.7x slower than C++ simdjson-dom and ~1.3x slower than sajson-dom in the same run; OCaml GC allocates significant minor/major words per parse (reported in the table) unlike the zero/near-zero-alloc C++ parsers; SIMD path is currently x86-oriented (SSE/AVX via ocaml_simd), no ARM NEON yet; error reporting is described by the author as still rudimentary; only the 'tape-reusable' variant beats RapidJSON — the plain simdjson-ox and non-reusable tape variants sit at or below RapidJSON's geomean.
caveats: Explicitly labeled by the author as a single-run, point-in-time snapshot, not a stable guarantee, and small differences should not be read as regressions without repeated interleaved measurements; very new project with only 3 stars.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fast json" language:ocaml

name: simdjson_nodejs
language: JavaScript (Node.js native addon binding to C++ simdjson)
workload: Parsing 15 standard JSON benchmark corpus files (apache_builds.json through update_center.json, including a 190MB sf_citylots.json) via a Node.js benchmark comparing JSON.parse against simdjson.lazyParse
claimed_speedup: 0.77x-2.30x vs JSON.parse depending on file; e.g. sf_citylots.json: 1492.166ms (JSON.parse) vs 709.692ms (simdjson.lazyParse) = ~2.10x faster (derived from page data); citm_catalog.json (0.93x) and twitter.json (0.77x) were slower than JSON.parse
tradeoffs: Overhead of converting the parsed C++ object into JS objects can make eager parse() slower than native JSON.parse; only the lazy-parse API is competitive; results are mixed across workloads (3 of 15 files were net slower in the published table); Node.js/V8 version and native-addon compiler flags are not stated.
caveats: Benchmark hardware is a 2018 laptop and no compiler/build flags for the native addon are given; project unmaintained since Feb 2023 (>3 years); results are not uniformly faster across the tested corpus, undermining a blanket 'faster' claim.

name: NetJSON
workload: Object serialize/deserialize round-trip benchmark (SimpleSpeedTester harness) comparing NetJSON against Json.NET, ServiceStack JSON, Jil, protobuf-net, JavaScriptSerializer and DataContractJsonSerializer
claimed_speedup: 3.4x faster than JSON.NET, 2.4x faster than ServiceStack JSON, 1.8x faster than Jil, 6x faster than JSON.NET BSON, 16.5x faster than Microsoft JavaScriptSerializer, 4.3x faster than DataContractJsonSerializer, 1.6x faster than protobuf-net (as stated verbatim in the project README, citing a linked 2014 third-party blog benchmark)
stars_or_usage: 238 stars; published on NuGet as NetJSON
tradeoffs: The cited numbers come from a single 2014 third-party blog post (theburningmonk.com) built on the author's own SimpleSpeedTester harness; that page presents results as charts rather than a machine-readable table and does not state CPU/hardware or .NET runtime version; the comparison predates System.Text.Json (shipped in .NET Core 3.0), so the modern .NET default serializer was never benchmarked against it.
caveats: Could not independently confirm the exact ratios as readable text/numbers on the linked blog page (chart-based, no CPU/runtime disclosed); benchmark methodology is over a decade old and the .NET JSON landscape has changed substantially since (System.Text.Json now ships in the runtime and is the modern incumbent).
